title: Modernizing Federal Reserve Operations in the 21st Century
summary: Fed Governor Christopher Waller delivered a speech at the Brookings Institution on April 21, 2026 outlining the historical evolution and ongoing modernization of Federal Reserve System operations. Waller, as the Board member responsible for Reserve Bank oversight, discussed the transition from a decentralized 'Bank first, System second' structure toward more centralized, efficient system-wide operations. The speech addressed fundamental questions about which Fed activities should remain locally organized versus consolidated across the System.
key_points: The Fed System consists of approximately 20,000 employees across 12 regional Reserve Banks, with the vast majority focused on operations including market operations, fiscal agent activities for Treasury, payment systems, and support functions
The original 1913 Federal Reserve Act created a decentralized structure as a political compromise between centralization and regional autonomy

Initially, all Reserve Bank activities were 'local' — including check processing, wire transactions, cash distribution, and local economic analysis — with each Bank self-contained and focused on its District

Key drivers of transformation included digitalization of financial transactions in the 1960s, Congress ending bank branching restrictions in the 1980s, and the emergence of national banking organizations that broke the one-to-one connection between Reserve Banks and member commercial banks
Statutory changes in 1935 gave Reserve Bank presidents a national role in monetary policy via the FOMC and 'nationalized' the discount rate across all Banks

Waller frames the central question as determining which activities are intrinsically local versus which can be conducted more efficiently system-wide through specialization, economies of scope, and economies of scale
The Conference of Presidents historically operated by consensus — they could not force any Bank to take action
